issues.legal_issue: Provision for the wakif or the wakif’s family is not a religious purpose merely because it is regarded as a pious act under Muslim law.
material_facts: The deeds provided for the maintenance or benefit of the wakifs’ families while also providing for charitable or religious expenditure.
The family-benefit provisions remained operative, and no religious worship, teaching, service, or performance of religious rites was involved in providing for the families.
issues.conclusion: The family provisions did not constitute religious purposes, and the deeds were not exclusively for religious purposes.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(n) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 defines religious purpose by reference to religious worship, teaching, service, or performance of religious rites. Under section 6(1)(i), the relevant holding must be exclusively for a religious or charitable purpose. Family maintenance does not become religious worship or a religious rite merely because it may be regarded as sadaqah or pious under Muslim law; the Court relied on the reasoning in Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Bussomoy Dhur Chowdry and Syed Mohiuddin Ahmed v. Sofia Khatun.

predicates.claim_under_retention_exemption: The proceeding involved a claim to retain property under an exemption from a property-vesting law.
predicates.family_or_self_support_provided: The trust or endowment provided benefits or maintenance for its founder or the founder’s family.
predicates.family_support_unconnected_to_religious_: The provision for the founder or family was not itself connected with religious worship, teaching, service, or performance of religious rites.

issues.definition: When a retention-exemption claim concerns a trust that provides for its founder or family outside religious rites, the family provision is not treated as a religious purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Private provision for the wakif or the wakif’s family is not a charitable purpose merely because Muslim law permits a family wakf.
material_facts: The deeds provided substantial continuing benefits for the wakifs’ families, including maintenance and other family allowances.
The deeds also directed expenditure toward charitable or religious purposes, but the family benefits were not shown to have ended or become inoperative.
The family provisions were not shown to be directed to poor or needy family members.
issues.conclusion: The family provisions were not charitable purposes because they were not relief of the poor, medical relief, advancement of education, or expenditure on an object of general public utility.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(c) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 includes relief of the poor, medical relief, advancement of education, and other objects of general public utility within charitable purpose. Section 6(1)(i) requires an exclusive charitable or religious purpose. The Court relied on Commissioners for Special Purposes of Income Tax v. Pemsel for the recognized heads of charity; Tribune Press Trustees, Lahore v. Income-tax Commissioner for the need to assess public benefit under the statutory test; D.V. Arur v. Commissioner of Income-tax and In re Mercantile Bank of India (Agency) Ltd. for the public-benefit requirement; and Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Bussomoy Dhur Chowdry, Syed Mohiuddin Ahmed v. Sofia Khatun, and Mujibunnissa v. Abdul Rahim for the conclusion that private family gifts are not charitable in the legal sense. The Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913 and the Shariat Act, 1937 did not give private family gifts a new meaning as charitable purposes.

rule.if: claim_under_retention_exemption and private_family_benefits_provided and family_benefits_not_for_poor_or_needy and no_general_public_benefit

predicates.claim_under_retention_exemption: The proceeding involved a claim to retain property under an exemption from a property-vesting law.
predicates.private_family_benefits_provided: The trust or endowment provided benefits for the founder or the founder’s family as private beneficiaries.
predicates.family_benefits_not_for_poor_or_needy: The family benefits were not limited to relieving poverty or meeting the needs of poor or needy beneficiaries.
predicates.no_general_public_benefit: The family provision did not serve an object of general public utility or otherwise confer the relevant public benefit.

issues.definition: A private family provision in a retention-exemption claim is not charitable when it is not directed to poor or needy beneficiaries and does not confer general public benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A trust with continuing, substantial secular or family benefits alongside charitable or religious purposes is not held exclusively for charitable or religious purposes.
material_facts: The deeds combined specified charitable or religious expenditure with substantial provisions for family maintenance and other family benefits.
The family provisions remained operative, and the appellants did not claim that the beneficiaries had been exhausted.
The governing statute applied notwithstanding contrary laws or instruments and provided an exemption only for property held exclusively for charitable or religious purposes.
issues.conclusion: The wakfs did not qualify for the exemption because their operative purposes included substantial secular and family purposes as well as charitable or religious purposes; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 4, and 5 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 provided for the Act’s overriding effect and the vesting of intermediaries’ estates and rights, while section 6(1)(i) allowed retention only where the relevant holding was exclusively for charitable or religious purposes. The word “exclusively” restricts the exemption to holdings solely within those purposes, and the exemption cannot be enlarged beyond the statutory words. The meanings of charitable and religious purpose are set by sections 2(c) and 2(n), respectively.

predicates.claim_under_retention_exemption: The proceeding involved a claim to retain property under an exemption from a property-vesting law.
predicates.charitable_or_religious_purposes_present: The trust or endowment provided for at least one charitable or religious purpose.
predicates.continuing_substantial_family_or_secular: The trust or endowment also provided substantial benefits for family members or other secular purposes.
predicates.family_or_secular_purposes_not_inoperati: The family or secular provisions remained operative rather than having ended or become inoperative.

issues.definition: A property-retention claim fails the exclusive-purpose test when charitable or religious purposes coexist with substantial, continuing family or secular purposes.
